newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end up sharply on Brazil port strike.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end up sharply on Brazil port strike.

text.p: CBOT soybeans settled sharply higher Monday on ideas that an impending Brazilian port strike would slow soy exports, loor traders said.
"If they happen to strike for a long time, we're going to have to ration beans," said one commission house trader.
World and U.S. supplies of soybeans are very low, so any disruption in supply has the potential to cause wild price fluctuations in the market, traders said.
Workers at the port of Paranagua voted to go on a 24-hour strike beginning Wednesday, and there is some concern that the action could spread to other ports.
However, some traders said the strike would most likely be settled quickly and loadings would soon return to normal.
Monday's gains sent March soybeans to a five-month high, which spurred new speculative buying, floor traders said. March's high of $8.12 equaled one set on September 23, 1996.
CBOT soybeans ended up 6-3/4 to 14-1/4 cents per bushel, with March up 14 at $8.05 a bushel and May up 14-1/4 at $8.07-1/2 per bushel.
Another supportive factor in Monday's trade was Friday's Commodity Futures Trading Commission report which showed a lighter-than-expected commodity fund long position, traders said.

The market shrugged off weaker-than-expected export shipment data. The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported Monday that export inspections totaled 13.786 million bushels. That figure compared with trade expectations for 23.0 to 26.0 million.
On the day, Rosenthal Collins sold three million bushels May, Smith Barney sold five million May, traders said, and Refco and Griffin Trading each bought two million May.
Volume was estimated at 70,000 contracts, above Friday's volume figure of 57,116 contracts, according to data from the CBOT.
